title: Out-of-order vs. in-order execution engine
decision: POWER4 implements out-of-order instruction execution with in-order retirement
rationale: out-of-order execution extracts more instruction-level parallelism by allowing instructions to execute when their operands are ready regardless of program order, thereby hiding memory latency and better utilizing execution units
outcome: POWER4 achieves significantly higher IPC than prior in-order IBM designs; the combination of out-of-order execution with in-order retirement maintains precise exceptions and simplifies the programming model
quote_as_recall_verbatim: out-of-order execution allows instructions to proceed as soon as their operands are available
weakest_point: my recall of the paper's specific framing of the in-order-alternative may conflate it with general POWER4 literature

title: Microarchitectural depth: longer pipeline for higher clock rate
where_in_paper: Pipeline organization and clock philosophy section
decision: POWER4 uses a deep pipelined design at 1.3-1.5 GHz rather than maximizing IPC at a lower frequency
alternatives_or_rejected: shorter pipeline with higher CPI (higher IPC per clock but lower absolute clock rate)
rationale: the paper argues that clock frequency is the primary driver of single-thread performance and that the market demanded higher frequency; cycle time improvements are weighed against IPC losses
outcome: POWER4 achieved approximately 1.3 GHz in initial silicon, representing a substantial clock-rate jump over POWER3, with acceptable CPI penalties from pipeline depth
weakest_point: the specific frequency numbers and the exact CPI vs. frequency trade-off analysis as presented in the paper - I am uncertain of the exact numbers and trade-off ratios the paper cites

title: L2 cache on-chip integration
decision: L2 cache is placed on the processor chip alongside the cores, not off-chip
alternatives_or_rejected: off-chip L2 (as in earlier IBM designs like POWER3)
rationale: on-chip L2 dramatically reduces latency and increases effective bandwidth; the paper notes that the off-chip L2 bus becomes a performance bottleneck at higher frequencies
outcome: POWER4 integrates 1.41 MB of L2 cache on-chip per processor, significantly reducing L2 access latency compared to off-chip alternatives
weakest_point: the exact L2 cache size (1.41 MB) and whether that specific number appears in this paper rather than in supplementary documentation

title: Extensive RAS hardware for commercial workloads
decision: POWER4 includes substantial redundant hardware: instruction retry, L1/L2 error correction codes (ECC), checkpoint repair, and extensive lockstep operation for fault detection
alternatives_or_rejected: minimal RAS with software-only recovery (higher performance, lower silicon area but unacceptable for commercial server market)
rationale: commercial workloads (database, ERP) require five-nines availability; the paper argues that hardware-level error detection and correction reduces planned and unplanned downtime, which is the primary concern of the target market
outcome: POWER4-based systems achieved high availability figures suitable for UNIX server market; the RAS features became a key differentiator against competitors
weakest_point: the specific RAS mechanisms listed here (checkpoint repair, lockstep specifics) - these may be in the paper but I am less certain of their exact names and implementations as described

title: Two-level branch predictor with selective history
decision: POWER4 implements a two-level adaptive branch predictor using a combination of global branch history register (GHR) and pattern history table (PHT)
rationale: two-level predictors more accurately capture correlated branch behavior in commercial workloads where branches have complex dependencies on prior branch outcomes
outcome: POWER4 achieved high branch prediction accuracy, reducing branch misprediction penalties which would otherwise severely impact performance due to the deep pipeline
weakest_point: the specific sizes of the GHR and PHT structures - these details may be in the paper or may be in the general POWER4 documentation, and I am uncertain which source they come from
